tagline: Railroad bridges found a second life carrying cars through the Keys.
intro: The Florida Keys Scenic Highway carries US 1 across islands and bridges for 110 miles. Florida’s scenic-highways program presents this All-American Road through its ocean vistas, coral reef and mangrove habitats. The designated corridor includes water for five miles on either side of the highway.

The idea began with the Miami Motor Club in 1921, when the club wanted to bring tourists to fishing areas then reached by boat or train. The first Overseas Highway opened in 1928 as two road sections joined by a 41-mile automobile ferry crossing. After the 1935 Labor Day hurricane damaged the Overseas Railroad, its owner could not afford to rebuild. Florida bought the railroad’s right-of-way and remaining infrastructure, and surviving bridges received wider concrete decks for cars. The continuous mainland-to-Key West highway opened in 1938.

Traveling south, begin north of Jewfish Creek Bridge and continue through Key Largo, Islamorada and Marathon toward the Lower Keys. US 1 has four lanes through Marathon; the Seven Mile Bridge connects the town with Little Duck Key. Beyond the bridge, the route crosses Bahia Honda and Big Pine Key, then continues through the Lower Keys and Stock Island. The scenic corridor ends at Mile Marker 0 in Old Town Key West.

moments.title: Islamorada
moments.text: At mile marker 82, Islamorada’s hurricane memorial contains the ashes of more than 300 victims of the 1935 Labor Day hurricane. The storm struck almost directly here while a highway bridge between Lower Matecumbe Key and Long Key was under construction. Among the hurricane’s more than 400 dead, over half were veterans and their families. The deaths prompted charges of mismanagement and a Congressional investigation. Farther along the highway at mile marker 73, eight concrete piers and a dredged island remain from the veterans’ bridge work. The unfinished piers also have a memorial plaque on Craig Key.

moments.title: Pigeon Key
moments.text: Pigeon Key held a work camp for Flagler’s railroad; buildings from its 1908–1912 construction era remain in the island’s historic district. The five-acre island includes a former Assistant Bridge Tender’s House converted into a museum of local artifacts and images. The old Seven Mile Bridge acquired an unusual detail when it became a road: discarded rails were painted white and reused as guardrails. The modern bridge, built from 1978 to 1982, bypasses Pigeon Key. The older approach to the island runs for 2.2 miles; its former swing span has been removed.

moments.title: Big Pine Key
moments.text: On Big Pine Key, signs along US 1 announce Key deer habitat and prohibit feeding the deer. The island holds the majority of the population of this small white-tailed deer subspecies. Its habitats include pine rocklands, hardwood hammocks, mangroves and freshwater wetlands. About two miles of US 1 at the island’s eastern end are elevated and fenced so deer can pass beneath the roadway. Road construction has also shaped a refuge landmark: the Blue Hole is an abandoned quarry used for road fill and Flagler’s railroad. Its mostly fresh water serves birds, snakes and alligators.
